title: Force
tagline: Understand turning effects, equilibrium and uniform circular motion.

overview.intro: Force in this chapter is studied through its turning effect, conditions for equilibrium and the dynamics of uniform circular motion. Concepts such as moment of a force, couple, centre of gravity and centripetal force connect everyday experiences like opening doors and balancing objects to examination problems. Clear understanding of vector direction, units and conditions for translational and rotational equilibrium is essential.

facts.value: Two equal, opposite, parallel forces producing rotation

learningOutcomes: Define moment of force and calculate it using perpendicular distance.
Explain couple, torque and conditions for rotational equilibrium.
Describe centre of gravity and factors affecting stability.

Explain uniform circular motion and the role of centripetal force.

learn.title: Moment of a Force and Turning Effect

blocks.text: The turning effect of a force about a pivot or axis is called the moment of the force (torque). It is defined as the product of the force and the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force. The SI unit is newton metre (N m), and the moment can be clockwise or anticlockwise depending on the direction of rotation produced.

For a given force, the moment increases if the perpendicular distance increases, which explains why door handles are placed far from hinges and why longer spanners make it easier to loosen nuts. When solving problems, always use the perpendicular distance, not the slant distance unless it equals the perpendicular.

items.text: A force of 10 N acts at 0.4 m perpendicular distance from a hinge: moment = 10 × 0.4 = 4 N m.
items.note: Multiply force by perpendicular distance only.

items.text: Pushing a door near the hinge requires more force than pushing near the edge.
items.note: Smaller distance means smaller moment for the same force.

blocks.text: A couple consists of two equal and opposite parallel forces whose lines of action do not coincide. A couple produces pure rotation without translation, and its moment is equal to one of the forces multiplied by the perpendicular distance between the forces. Turning a steering wheel or opening a tap with two fingers are common examples.

A body is in equilibrium when it remains at rest or in uniform motion under the action of forces. For complete equilibrium, two conditions must be satisfied: the resultant force must be zero (translational equilibrium) and the algebraic sum of moments about any point must be zero (rotational equilibrium). The principle of moments is applied in balancing beams and levers.

items: Clockwise and anticlockwise moments must balance for rotational equilibrium.
Resultant force zero prevents linear acceleration.
A couple cannot be balanced by a single force, only by another couple.
Choose a convenient pivot to simplify moment calculations.

blocks.text: The centre of gravity (CG) of a body is the point through which the resultant weight of the body acts for all orientations. For regular, uniform objects, the CG lies at the geometric centre, while for irregular objects it may be located experimentally by suspension methods. The position of CG influences how a body balances.

Stability of a body depends on the position of its centre of gravity and the size of its base. A lower centre of gravity and a wider base increase stability because the line of action of weight is more likely to fall within the base when the body is tilted. Racing cars and conical flasks illustrate these principles.

items.meaning: The point where the entire weight of a body may be considered to act.
A state in which a displaced body returns to its original position.
For equilibrium, sum of clockwise moments equals sum of anticlockwise moments about the same point.

blocks.text: When a body moves in a circular path with constant speed, it is said to be in uniform circular motion. Although speed is constant, velocity changes continuously because direction changes at every point. This change in velocity implies acceleration directed towards the centre of the circle, called centripetal acceleration.

A centripetal force is required to keep the body moving in a circular path and always acts towards the centre. It is not a new type of force but is provided by tension, friction, gravity or normal reaction depending on the situation. If the centripetal force ceases, the body moves tangentially due to inertia.

Problems on moments often involve finding unknown forces or distances by applying the principle of moments. Diagrams should show all forces, distances and pivot points clearly. Distinguish between mass and weight where necessary, using W = mg when converting mass to force.

In circular motion questions, identify the force providing centripetal acceleration and state its direction. Remember that centrifugal force is a pseudo force observed in a rotating frame and is not an outward force acting on the body in an inertial frame. Correct terminology helps avoid conceptual errors.

items: Always state units: N m for moment, N for force, m for distance.
Use perpendicular distances in moment calculations.
Check equilibrium by considering both forces and moments.
Centripetal force acts towards the centre, not along the tangent.

keyPoints: Moment of a force equals force multiplied by perpendicular distance from pivot.
A couple produces rotation and its moment is F × perpendicular distance between forces.
For equilibrium, resultant force and resultant moment must both be zero.
Principle of moments balances clockwise and anticlockwise moments about the same point.
Centre of gravity is the point where the weight of a body effectively acts.
Lower centre of gravity and wider base increase stability.
Uniform circular motion has constant speed but changing velocity due to changing direction.
Centripetal force acts towards the centre and is provided by an existing force.
Use SI units and perpendicular distances in all calculations.
Clear free-body thinking helps identify forces and turning effects.

questions.prompt: The SI unit of moment of a force is:
questions.answer: newton metre
questions.explanation: Moment is force multiplied by perpendicular distance, so its SI unit is N m.
questions.commonMistake: Joule is also N m but is used for work/energy, not moment.

questions.prompt: A body in uniform circular motion has constant:
questions.answer: speed
questions.explanation: In uniform circular motion speed is constant but velocity changes due to continuous change in direction.
questions.commonMistake: Velocity is a vector and changes even when speed is constant.

questions.prompt: Centripetal force acts:
questions.answer: towards the centre
questions.explanation: Centripetal force is always directed towards the centre of the circular path.
questions.commonMistake: Tangential direction relates to instantaneous velocity, not centripetal force.

questions.prompt: A couple produces:
questions.answer: only rotation
questions.explanation: Equal and opposite parallel forces of a couple create a turning effect without resultant linear force.
questions.commonMistake: A single force can cause translation; a couple causes pure rotation.

questions.prompt: For a body to be in equilibrium:
options: both resultant force and resultant moment must be zero
resultant force must be zero only
resultant moment must be zero only
questions.answer: both resultant force and resultant moment must be zero
questions.explanation: Complete equilibrium requires no linear acceleration and no rotational acceleration.
questions.commonMistake: Zero force alone does not prevent rotation by a couple.

questions.prompt: The stability of a body increases when its:
questions.answer: centre of gravity is lowered
questions.explanation: A lower centre of gravity makes it harder for the line of action of weight to fall outside the base.
questions.commonMistake: A wider base also increases stability; a narrow base reduces it.

questions.prompt: The moment of a 20 N force acting at a perpendicular distance of 0.3 m from a pivot is:
questions.answer: 6 N m
questions.explanation: Moment = force × perpendicular distance = 20 × 0.3 = 6 N m.
questions.commonMistake: Multiply, do not divide or add the values.

questions.prompt: If the string breaks while whirling a stone in a horizontal circle, the stone moves:
options: along the tangent at that point
questions.answer: along the tangent at that point
questions.explanation: Without centripetal force, the stone continues in the direction of its instantaneous velocity due to inertia.
questions.commonMistake: There is no outward force pulling it radially away in an inertial frame.

questions.prompt: The turning effect of a force is called the ________ of the force.
questions.answer: moment
questions.explanation: Moment (or torque) measures the rotational effect of a force about a pivot.
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse moment with momentum.

questions.prompt: In uniform circular motion, the force directed towards the centre is called ________ force.
questions.answer: centripetal
questions.explanation: Centripetal force maintains circular motion by continuously changing the direction of velocity.
questions.commonMistake: Centrifugal is not the real inward force in an inertial frame.

questions.prompt: For rotational equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of ________ moments.
questions.answer: anticlockwise
questions.explanation: This is the principle of moments applied about the same point.
questions.commonMistake: Moments must be taken about the same pivot.

questions.prompt: Define moment of a force and state its SI unit.
questions.answer: The moment of a force about a point is the product of the force and the perpendicular distance of its line of action from the point. Its SI unit is newton metre (N m).
questions.explanation: Perpendicular distance is essential in the definition.
questions.commonMistake: Do not omit the word perpendicular in the definition.

questions.prompt: Why is it easier to open a door by pushing at its edge rather than near the hinges?
questions.answer: Pushing at the edge increases the perpendicular distance from the hinges (pivot), so a smaller force produces the same moment. Near the hinges the distance is small, requiring a larger force for the same turning effect.
questions.explanation: Moment depends directly on perpendicular distance for a given force.
questions.commonMistake: Relate the explanation to moment, not just effort.

questions.prompt: State the two conditions for the equilibrium of a rigid body.
questions.answer: (1) The vector sum of all forces acting on the body must be zero, ensuring translational equilibrium. (2) The algebraic sum of moments of all forces about any point must be zero, ensuring rotational equilibrium.
questions.explanation: Both conditions are necessary for complete equilibrium.
questions.commonMistake: Mentioning only one condition is insufficient.

questions.prompt: What provides the centripetal force in (i) a car taking a circular turn on a level road and (ii) the Moon revolving around the Earth?
questions.answer: (i) Friction between the tyres and the road provides the centripetal force towards the centre of the turn. (ii) Gravitational attraction between the Earth and the Moon provides the centripetal force towards the Earth.
questions.explanation: Centripetal force is supplied by an existing physical force in each situation.
questions.commonMistake: State the actual force and its direction towards the centre.

questions.prompt: Explain the principle of moments and describe how it is used to find an unknown weight using a metre rule.
questions.answer: The principle of moments states that for a body in rotational equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about the same point. To find an unknown weight, suspend a metre rule at its centre so it balances horizontally. Hang a known weight on one side and the unknown weight on the other, adjusting positions until the rule balances. Then, known weight × its distance from pivot = unknown weight × its distance from pivot, allowing the unknown weight to be calculated.
questions.explanation: Balancing ensures equal and opposite moments about the pivot.
questions.commonMistake: Measure distances from the pivot, not from the ends of the rule.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between uniform linear motion and uniform circular motion with reference to speed, velocity and acceleration.
questions.answer: In uniform linear motion, a body moves in a straight line with constant speed and constant direction, so velocity is constant and acceleration is zero. In uniform circular motion, a body moves in a circular path with constant speed but continuously changing direction, so velocity changes at every instant. This change in velocity produces centripetal acceleration directed towards the centre of the circle, requiring a centripetal force.
questions.explanation: Direction change in circular motion is the key difference affecting velocity and acceleration.
questions.commonMistake: Do not say velocity is constant in uniform circular motion.

questions.prompt: A uniform metre rule balances at the 50 cm mark. A 2 N weight is hung at the 20 cm mark. Where should a 3 N weight be hung to balance the rule?
questions.answer: The pivot is at 50 cm. The 2 N weight at 20 cm is 30 cm (0.30 m) from the pivot on one side, producing an anticlockwise moment of 2 × 30 = 60 N cm. For equilibrium, clockwise moment must be 60 N cm. Let the 3 N weight be placed at distance d cm from the pivot on the other side: 3 × d = 60, so d = 20 cm. Therefore the 3 N weight should be hung at 50 + 20 = 70 cm mark.
questions.explanation: Equal clockwise and anticlockwise moments about the pivot give balance.
questions.commonMistake: Add the distance to the pivot position to find the scale mark on the correct side.

questions.prompt: A door requires a moment of 12 N m to open. If the handle is 0.8 m from the hinges, calculate the minimum force needed when applied perpendicular to the door. Why is this force larger if applied closer to the hinges?
questions.answer: Moment = force × perpendicular distance, so force = moment/distance = 12/0.8 = 15 N. If the force is applied closer to the hinges, the perpendicular distance decreases, and since the required moment is the same, the force must increase (force = 12/d).
questions.explanation: Inverse relationship between force and distance for a fixed moment explains the difference.
questions.commonMistake: Use the perpendicular distance from hinges in all cases.

questions.prompt: Explain why passengers in a bus feel pushed outward when the bus takes a sharp turn, using the concept of inertia and centripetal force.
questions.answer: When the bus turns, it changes direction due to a centripetal force (friction) acting on it towards the centre of the curve. Passengers tend to continue in their original straight-line motion due to inertia. Relative to the turning bus, this appears as an outward push. In an inertial frame, there is no real outward force on passengers; instead, a centripetal force is needed (e.g. from the seat or handhold) to make them turn with the bus.
questions.explanation: The sensation arises from inertia while the frame of reference accelerates.
questions.commonMistake: Avoid describing centrifugal force as a real force in the inertial frame.

questions.prompt: A see-saw is balanced with a child of weight 300 N sitting 2 m from the pivot. Another child sits 1.5 m from the pivot on the opposite side. Find the weight of the second child. If the second child moves closer to the pivot, what happens to balance?
questions.answer: For balance, clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment. Taking moments about the pivot: 300 × 2 = W × 1.5, so 600 = 1.5W and W = 400 N. The second child’s weight is 400 N. If the second child moves closer to the pivot, their distance decreases, reducing their moment (400 × smaller distance < 600 N m). The see-saw will tilt down on the first child’s side unless the second child moves back or a greater weight is applied.
questions.explanation: Balance depends on equality of moments; changing distance changes the moment.
questions.commonMistake: Recalculate or reason using the moment equation when distance changes.

questions.prompt: Why is a low centre of gravity important in the design of a racing car? Explain using stability principles.
questions.answer: A racing car with a low centre of gravity is more stable, especially when taking sharp turns at high speed. When the car tilts, the line of action of its weight is more likely to remain within the base formed by its wheels. This prevents the turning moment due to weight from toppling the car. A wider wheelbase further increases stability, but lowering the centre of gravity is crucial for safe cornering.
questions.explanation: Stability depends on keeping the weight’s line of action within the support base.
questions.commonMistake: Link the explanation to the line of action of weight and base width, not just speed.
